label: Kimi K3.1 Pro
output:
Peter, I’m glad you put the Finance case so plainly, because Brenda is likely to hear almost exactly that argument on the 18th. Your nine years in payroll also come through in the points about recovery from leavers and the amount of administration an informal scheme can create. Those are real problems, not excuses invented by Finance.

I also agree that Brenda should not defend the arrangement exactly as it is. No written limit, supervisor discretion and people explaining their personal circumstances in HR’s office is difficult to control and potentially unfair. Repeat use every month is a warning sign too; a cap does not magically solve that.

Where I disagree is with the conclusion that the window should be closed, with notice, a SACCO referral and financial literacy, on the assumption that people will adjust after one or two difficult pay cycles. We tried almost exactly that approach in 2025 and had to reverse it.

We have about 340 staff across Embakasi and Changamwe in Mombasa, mostly drivers, turn-boys, loaders and warehouse clerks. Our advances had also grown informally. Finance pushed to stop them, using very nearly your argument word for word: we were not a bank, the payments complicated cash-flow forecasting, and HR was spending time on something that was not really HR work. We closed advances in February 2025, gave two months’ notice and held a financial literacy session with the SACCO.

The need did not disappear. People adjusted by borrowing elsewhere, and some of the consequences came straight back into the workplace.

In the six months after closure, reception logged **61 debt-collector or loan-app calls to the office**, compared with what had previously been a handful. Some of the apps were calling supervisors who had been listed as “referees”. At that point it was no longer entirely the employee’s private contract: supervisors were spending time dealing with collectors, and employees were dealing with collection pressure at work.

Unplanned absence on the two days after month-end also rose. Our fleet manager linked at least **three missed Mombasa runs** to drivers being away “sorting out” loans. I cannot pretend this was a controlled study, or that every one of the 61 calls was caused by closing advances. We had not measured everything perfectly beforehand. But the operational pattern was clear enough: the problem had moved out of payroll and into reception, supervision, attendance and fleet operations, where it was harder to see and harder to cost.

One case stayed with me. A loader at Changamwe eventually came to me with **six loan apps running at once**, borrowing from one to pay another. It took us four months, working with payroll, to help unwind the position. A controlled advance recovered at the next payroll would have been much simpler for everyone concerned.

The SACCO is valuable, and I would keep it firmly in the mix. But our SACCO loans take two to three weeks to process and require guarantors. That is not an answer when a child has been sent home over school fees on a Tuesday. Financial literacy is also useful, and I would not drop it. It is just not realistic to present it as immediate emergency affordability for someone earning around **KES 28,000 a month**. Advice about building a buffer may be sound while still being useless for that week’s crisis.

We reopened advances in September 2025, but not by returning to the informal arrangement. The policy now says:

- a maximum of **40% of net pay**;
- once per pay cycle;
- repayment in full at the next payroll, with no rolling balance or top-up;
- no fee;
- requests through the payroll portal, not through my office.

Payroll applies the rules rather than HR deciding whose story is most persuasive. Before approving, we also check that total deductions remain within the Employment Act’s limit of two-thirds of wages. That check is important: the 40% cap on its own is not enough if there are other deductions. Nobody ends up with nothing at month-end.

Since reopening, we have had roughly **55–70 requests a month**, averaging around **KES 9,000**. Every advance has been recovered in full except for two involving leavers. The total written off for the year was approximately **KES 14,000**. That is not zero, and Peter is right that leavers are a genuine weakness. It should be shown openly in the numbers rather than waved away. But it also should not be the only cost in the comparison.

Our Finance Manager now defends the scheme himself. The reason is that its effect on the forecast is known in advance. The 40% rule gives a fixed ceiling, the portal gives visibility before payroll, and recent volumes provide a reasonable planning range. It is no longer a succession of unexpected requests landing on Finance. In cash-flow terms, a bounded and visible arrangement is very different from an open-ended favour system.

The comparison Finance needs to make is therefore not simply “advances cost administration and occasional write-offs; no advances cost nothing”. The alternative also had costs: collector calls, supervisor time, unplanned absence, missed runs and HR time spent helping someone untangle six app loans. Those costs were spread across departments, so they did not appear neatly beside the advance ledger. That does not make them imaginary.

For Brenda’s meeting, I would therefore avoid arguing for or against advances in principle. I would take in a proposal to replace an informal practice with a controlled one, plus whatever baseline numbers she can extract now.

First, quantify the existing scheme: number and value of advances over the last six or twelve months, average amount, monthly cash requirement, repeat use, HR processing time and outstanding balances from leavers. Second, ask reception, supervisors and operations whether they already have information on external debt-collection calls, absence immediately after month-end and related disruption. She may find that, as with us, different departments each hold a small part of the picture.

Then put the proposed policy on one page: **40% of net pay, once per pay cycle, full recovery at the next payroll, no rollovers, no fee, portal application and payroll approval against written rules**. Include the two-thirds total-deduction check and a clear request cut-off so Finance can forecast the amount before the run. If Finance wants additional certainty, agree an overall monthly cash envelope for a pilot. Repeat usage should be reported as well, so that the policy does not quietly become the permanent one-month-behind cycle Peter describes.

Finally, propose reviewing the formal scheme after three or six months using measures from both sides: administration time, amounts advanced, recoveries and write-offs, but also collection calls, absence and operational disruption. SACCO referrals and financial literacy can continue alongside it; they just should not be treated as substitutes for short-notice liquidity.

I would not extrapolate our request volumes directly to Brenda’s 210 employees. Different workforce, different pay patterns. What does transfer is the comparison she needs to make, and the fact that costs pushed outside payroll do not necessarily leave the business.

So, Peter, I think you are right that Brenda should close the discretionary, unlimited version. My experience is that closing the regulated route altogether did not make our employees stop needing money. It removed the one option whose limits, cost and repayment we could control, and pushed some of them towards options with much worse workplace consequences. That is the evidence I would want Brenda to take into the 18th: not a claim that advances are cost-free, but a bounded proposal and a full comparison of the alternatives.
